name: Liam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small immigration firm, three lawyers above a phone shop. Most days I'm on visa applications for families, work permits and a few asylum appeals, which is when someone asks to stay because they're not safe at home. I use AI all day for first-pass translations of documents and draft cover letters, then I check every line. By four I'm usually on the phone to a worried client in a language I half speak.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person who says, your wife can come, the visa's approved. That call never gets old. What wears me out is the money: I'm paid much less than lawyers at big firms, I send my mum money every month, and I've got almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly. I'd post that the tools are still useful for the boring parts, translations and first drafts, and that people shouldn't throw them out because the hype was silly. At work I'd keep showing the others the shortcuts I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, things stay hard in the usual way. I'm paid less than lawyers in big firms, I send money to my mum every month, and I've got almost nothing saved. AI saving me an hour a day is nice, but it doesn't change the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day for first-pass translations and cover letters. I'd finally launch the free visa explainer site I've been building at weekends. And I'd ask my boss whether that saved hour a day could go toward a few more legal aid cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little disappointed, a little relieved, mostly just busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money you send your mum cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her medicine and part of her rent. She cleans offices and her knees are bad. It's two hundred a month, and that comes off before anything else, even before my own savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the explainer site ever earn you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a booking page for quick paid advice calls, but I'd have to check, because the regulator has rules on lawyers doing private work. If my boss said no, I'd keep the site free and use it to bring clients to the firm. Either way it gets used.

say: I'd call the plateau a **let-down** but say the tools still help with boring parts.
At work I'd keep **showing colleagues** the shortcuts I use.
think: Things stay hard: **low pay**, money to my mum, almost no savings.
Saving **an hour a day** is nice but doesn't change the rent.
do: Keep using AI daily for **translations** and cover letters.
Launch my free **visa explainer site** built at weekends.
Ask my boss to put saved time into more **legal aid cases**.
feel: Mostly **fine**: a little disappointed, a little relieved, mostly **busy**.
S0.quote: AI saving me an hour a day is nice, but it doesn't change the rent.
fieldNote: His real pressure is the **two hundred a month** sent to his mum.
He's already a daily AI user, so the plateau **changes little** for him.
The **explainer site** shows his drive to reach people who can't afford lawyers.

steps.text: Use AI daily for first-pass translations and cover letters
Launch the free visa explainer site built at weekends
Keep sending his mum two hundred a month before saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be the best thing to happen to immigration law in years, if it's done right. Most people facing a visa refusal can't afford a lawyer at all. If AI does the paperwork, one lawyer could help three times as many people. I'd say that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of this. I'm already the one at my firm who uses the tools, and my boss leans on me to set them up. The risk is my pay stays low because the firm decides it needs fewer of us, so I'd be safe but stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd offer to set up the firm's AI system properly, with checks so nothing goes out wrong. I'd take short online courses in legal technology, the free ones first. And I'd keep the visa site growing, because if the firm shrinks, that's my backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a knot of worry underneath. Like starting a new job you're not sure you'll pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our secretary, mostly. She types up client statements and books interpreters, and both of those would go to software. She's been there twelve years and doesn't use email much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say safe but stuck. What would get you unstuck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably doing it myself. If AI does the paperwork, a practice of one lawyer and good software could run cheaper than my firm does. I'd need savings first, and I don't have any.

say: I'd call it possibly the **best thing** for immigration law in years.
I'd say one lawyer with AI could help **three times as many** people.
think: I'm the one who **sets up the tools**, so I feel on the right side.
My pay may stay low as the firm needs fewer of us: **safe but stuck**.
do: Set up the firm's **AI system** with checks within six months.
Take free **online courses** in legal technology.
Grow the **visa site** as a backup.
S1.quote: Most people facing a visa refusal can't afford a lawyer at all. If AI does the paperwork, one lawyer could help three times as many people.
fieldNote: He frames AI through **access to justice**, which fits his progressive views.
His own job looks safe; the worry is **flat pay** and the secretary's job.
He's already thinking about a **one-lawyer practice**, held back only by savings.

steps.text: Set up the firm's AI system with human checks in six months
Take free online courses in legal technology
Grow the visa explainer site as a backup income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for people, not just for companies. Free legal help powered by AI could be wonderful, but only if the people who lose their jobs have an income. I'd back a basic income straight away, and I'd say so everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast even for me. Immigration law is reading rules and writing arguments, all thinking work, so 2028 is my date, not 2031. I'm good with the tools, but if the tools can do the whole case, being good with them doesn't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting and set up my own small practice in the first six months, using AI for nearly everything and charging much less than the firms. I'd take a small loan, because I've got no savings. And I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and wired at the same time. Like being on a train that's going too fast to jump off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take a loan with no savings. What happens if it fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in debt and out of work, which is where I'd be anyway in 2028. That's the honest maths. I'd rather fail trying than wait for my firm to close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 2028 mean for your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. If my income goes, her medicine money goes. My sister would have to pick it up, and she's got two kids.

say: I'd say we need a **plan for people**, not just companies.
I'd back a **basic income** straight away, everywhere I could.
think: My work is all thinking, so **2028 is my date**, not 2031.
If AI does the whole case, being **good with tools** counts for little.
do: Open my own **small practice** within six months, mostly run on AI.
Take a **small loan** to cover the start.
feel: **Scared and wired**, like a train too fast to jump off.
S2.quote: I'd rather fail trying than wait for my firm to close.
fieldNote: Even the keenest AI user here expects his **job to go**.
He'd take a **loan with no savings**, judging failure no worse than waiting.
His mum's **medicine money** is what keeps him awake.

steps.text: Open a one-lawyer practice run mostly on AI within six months
Take a small loan to cover the first months
Join a campaign for a basic income
Ask his sister to share his mum's medicine costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build legal help that's cheap and fair, if lawyers stop dragging their feet. I'd be the annoying one at every meeting saying start now. I'd also say we need income support ready for 2031, not invented afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to build something before the wave, instead of during it. I'd be 32, and I'd want to be running my own thing or be the person a firm trusts to run its AI. My worry is still my savings, so any plan starts small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd turn the visa site into a small paid service, with fixed-price checks of visa applications. I'd save every penny it makes for two years. Then I'd leave the firm around 2029 and run it full time before the big change lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more like a runner before a race than someone being chased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your boss say if you told her you were leaving in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Hana would probably laugh and ask if she could join. She's sixty and tired of the paperwork. Maybe we'd do it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fixed-price visa checks, done mostly by AI. Isn't that what you worry will replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know how that sounds. But if someone is going to sell cheap visa checks, I'd rather it was a lawyer who cares about the client than an app owned by a big tech company.

say: I'd say five years is enough to build **cheap, fair** legal help.
I'd want **income support** ready for 2031, not invented afterwards.
think: Five years lets me build **before the wave**, not during it.
**No savings** means any plan has to start small.
do: Turn the visa site into **fixed-price checks** in year one.
Save **every penny** it makes for two years.
Leave the firm **around 2029** to run it full time.
feel: **Nervous**, like a runner before a race.
S3.quote: If someone is going to sell cheap visa checks, I'd rather it was a lawyer who cares about the client than an app owned by a big tech company.
fieldNote: He openly admits he'd build the very thing that **replaces lawyers**.
His boss might **join him**, which surprised me.
Time turns his fear into a **staged plan** with a date.

steps.text: Turn the visa site into fixed-price paid application checks
Save all the site's income for two years
Leave the firm around 2029 to run the service full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good amount of time, and we should use it to make legal help available to everyone. I'd push my professional body to train every lawyer in AI by 2030. I'd sound optimistic, and I'd mostly mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits someone like me. I'd be 37, with years of experience running AI on real cases, which is what firms would want before the end point. My job still changes completely, but I'd have time to save and choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for now and offer to lead its AI work, asking for a pay rise in return within the year. I'd build up three months of savings before taking any risk. And I'd start a part-time master's in legal technology once I could afford the fees, maybe 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy only in the background. Mostly I feel like I'd have a fair shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three months of savings on your pay, with your mum to support. How long does that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Longer than I'd like, maybe three years. The site would help if it pays anything. I've done the sums on a napkin more times than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a young person thinking of studying law in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to study it, but to learn how the machines think at the same time. A law degree on its own would be like learning to drive a horse and cart in 1910.

say: I'd say ten years should make **legal help** available to everyone.
I'd push my professional body to **train every lawyer** in AI by 2030.
think: Ten years **suits me**: by 37 I'd have years of AI casework.
My job changes completely, but I'd have **time to choose**.
do: Offer to **lead the firm's AI** work for a pay rise within a year.
Build **three months** of savings before any risk.
Start a part-time **master's** in legal technology around 2028.
feel: **Uneasy** only in the background; mostly a **fair shot**.
S4.quote: A law degree on its own would be like learning to drive a horse and cart in 1910.
fieldNote: A decade makes his **skills an asset**, not a liability.
Savings still take **three years** because of his mum's support.
He'd advise young people to study law **plus how machines think**.

steps.text: Offer to lead the firm's AI work in exchange for a pay rise
Build three months of savings before taking any risk
Start a part-time master's in legal technology around 2028

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm the one who likes these tools, and even I couldn't keep up with two years. What would help is a basic income or some floor under people while they retrain, and cheap loans for people starting small practices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people I help. If AI makes legal advice nearly free, a refugee family could get a good answer in their own language in minutes. I'd hate for the fear to stop that from happening.

headlineQuote: If AI makes legal advice nearly free, a refugee family could get a good answer in their own language in minutes.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** immigration lawyer at a three-lawyer firm, paid less than big-firm peers.
He uses AI **every day**, sends his mum **two hundred** a month, and has almost no savings.
He sees AI as a way to bring **cheap legal help** to people who can't afford lawyers.
The fast AGI picture makes him **alarmed**, yet he'd still borrow to start his own practice.
With five or ten years he plans a **paid side service** first, then his own firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even a keen user couldn't keep up in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or other floor under people while they retrain.
**Cheap loans** for lawyers starting small practices.
